Pico 3

Shunsuke Kakita, Rajul Basnet
Cornerstone of Engineering – Fall 2026
Overview

What is this project?

In this project, we worked together to create a speed sensor. Prior to creating the speed sensor, we did preliminary tasks to showcase each component of the project, both individually and in combination.

Goals

Goals of the project

  • Task 1 – Using the ultrasonic distance sensor and seeing its functions
  • Task 2 – Using the obstacle avoidance module and seeing its functions
  • Task 3 – Using active and passive buzzers and seeing their functions
  • Task 4 – Using an LCD display and seeing its functions
  • Build a speed sensor
How It Works

How it works

Step 01

For this first task, I used the ultrasonic distance sensor to see how it reads distance in real time. The code takes into account that the sensor uses sound waves in order to detect distance. Relating the time it takes for the sound it emits to come back determines the distance.

Step 02

For this second task, I used the infrared obstacle avoidance module to detect whether something was in front of it. The sensor shines invisible infrared light, and if an object is close enough, the light bounces back into a receiver on the module.

Step 03

For this third task, I used passive and active buzzers. Both were connected to the same circuit, with a transistor acting as a switch because the Pico can’t power a buzzer directly. The code first turns the buzzer on and off every second, then switches it on and off to make a tone, and finally plays four different pitches.

Step 04

For this fourth task, I used an LCD screen to show text without needing the computer. The code first searches for the screen and prints its address, then sets up the screen and displays my name on the top row and my section on the bottom row.

Step 05

For this code, AI was used for help with the speed calculations and display. The code works by taking the readings from each sensor, putting them into the speed formula – then when certain boundaries are triggered, the LEDs change color correspondingly. For this, we set the speed limit to be 5 – turning yellow at or above that value. The LED is red when the obstacle sensor detects the object, which means it is getting too close.

How It Was Made

How it was made

Step 01

We wired the distance module to each of its respective pins, using resistors to connect them. The setup was fairly simple, connecting the component to the Pico using its pins.

Step 02

This was made by connecting the corresponding functions into the assigned Pico pins.

Step 03

Following the same setup from task 1, we incorporated a buzzer for instances with both active and passive. For the setup, the buzzer’s wiring was also connected to its respective Pico pins with resistors.

Step 04

This was made by connecting the corresponding functions into the assigned Pico pins.

Step 05

This circuit combined what the preliminary tasks showcased, connecting each of the corresponding pins to the Pico for each component. For the distance sensor, we used AI help to formulate a split-voltage connection through the trig pin. The reference object used was the box, as seen in the video. The obstacle sensor was floppy, so to demonstrate, we put it close to the object to showcase the red LED.
